hints: Focus on the last step, where a white precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH to give a solution. That is a very special property.
Recall which metal hydroxide is amphoteric and dissolves in excess alkali to form a soluble complex ion, starting from its oxide dissolving in HCl.
Check which element burns to give an amphoteric white oxide that fits the whole chain from oxide to chloride to hydroxide to aluminate.
walkthrough:
**Spot the key clue at the end**

The most telling step is white precipitate + excess NaOH(aq) goes to solution. This means the hydroxide is amphoteric, it reacts with both acids and bases.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{amphoteric hydroxide} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{soluble complex ion}$$

**Test aluminium through the sequence**

Aluminium burns to white aluminium oxide, which dissolves in HCl to give a solution of aluminium chloride.

Equations:
$$4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \text{ (white solid)}$$
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (solution)}$$

**Form the precipitate then redissolve it**

Adding NaOH gives white aluminium hydroxide precipitate, and excess NaOH dissolves it to give the soluble tetrahydroxoaluminate ion.

Equations:
$$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Al}(\text{OH})_3 \text{ (white precipitate)}$$
$$\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow [\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]^- \text{ (solution)}$$

**Conclude the identity of Y**

Only aluminium fits every stage, especially the dissolving of the white precipitate in excess alkali. So Y must be Al.

options.A: Aluminium fits perfectly. It forms white amphoteric Al2O3, which dissolves in HCl to AlCl3 solution, then gives white Al(OH)3 precipitate with NaOH, which dissolves in excess NaOH to form soluble [Al(OH)4]-.
options.B: Calcium burns to white CaO and gives CaCl2 solution, then white Ca(OH)2 precipitate, but Ca(OH)2 is basic, not amphoteric, so it does not dissolve in excess NaOH to give a solution.
options.C: Magnesium burns to white MgO and gives MgCl2 solution, then white Mg(OH)2 precipitate, but Mg(OH)2 is basic only and is insoluble in excess NaOH, so the final solution would not form.
options.D: Phosphorus burns to white P4O10, which is acidic and dissolves to give acidic phosphoric acid solution. It would not give a white hydroxide precipitate with NaOH, only soluble sodium phosphate salts.
